text: Beleaguered means beset with troubles from every direction at once — struggling, under pressure, hit from all sides. The article calls 23andMe a “beleaguered” company because it was already in deep trouble when hackers stole the genetic data of 6.9 million of its customers — bad news piled on top of bad news.

To accrue is to build up gradually over time, bit by bit — the way interest slowly stacks up in a savings account. Here the point is who the payoff lands on: the benefits of the medical research “accrue to other people,” meaning they trickle in years later and often help strangers, not the baby whose DNA was actually tested.

Purgatory is a miserable in-between state of waiting, stuck between two outcomes with no clear answer — the word comes from an old religious idea of a place between heaven and hell. “Diagnostic purgatory” is what parents fall into when a test says their child might have a disease but can't say for sure: no diagnosis, no all-clear, just months of worry.

Mission creep is when a project quietly grows past what it was first meant to do — no one ever decides to expand it, it just spreads. The worry here is that a programme sold to parents as simple disease-screening for their baby secretly balloons into a permanent DNA databank for research, so you “can't take part in one without taking part in the other.”

To sequence DNA is to read out the exact order of the chemical “letters” that make up a person's genetic code — like transcribing a book one letter at a time. The whole article asks whether every newborn should have this done, since sequencing reveals far more about your health (and your risks) than an ordinary blood test.

Your genome is your complete set of DNA — the full instruction manual for building and running your body, written in genes. Because a genome is so personal and permanent, storing one “indefinitely” is exactly what makes some parents nervous: it can never be changed and could reveal secrets you didn't ask to know.

Penetrance is a genetics term for how often a risky gene actually causes the disease it's linked to — the fraction of people carrying a “disease gene” who really get sick. It's the article's central idea: a gene once thought to cause eye cancer over 90% of the time turned out, in a newer study, to do so in fewer than a third of carriers. High-sounding risk, much lower reality.

A mutation is a change or “typo” in a gene — sometimes harmless, sometimes the cause of a disease. DNA sequencing can flag disease-causing mutations early, but it also flags many that may never actually make you ill, which is where a lot of the needless worry in this story comes from.

A genetic variant is simply a version of a gene that differs from the common one — some are “risky variants” linked to disease. The catch the article keeps returning to: carrying a risky variant raises your odds of a problem, but plenty of people carry one and stay perfectly healthy their whole lives.

Here a marker isn't something you write with — it's a biological clue, a telltale sign in the blood or DNA that points to a particular disease. Older screening tests look for “markers of conditions such as sickle-cell anaemia,” checking a blood sample for those warning signs.

To fret is to worry — to stew and fuss over something anxiously. The article says critics “fret” that sequencing every baby's DNA could cause needless alarm and force parents to hand over deeply private data.

Saying “genes are not always destiny” means your DNA sets the odds, not the outcome — it isn't a fixed fate you can't escape. Environment, other genes, and plain luck all get a vote, which is why most people carrying a disease-linked gene never actually develop that disease.

Middling means middle-of-the-road — not high, not low, just so-so. Testing for genes with “low or middling penetrance” means testing for genes that only sometimes lead to illness, which is exactly what leaves families stuck worrying about a problem that may never come.

Inflating here has nothing to do with pumping up a balloon — it means making a number look bigger than it really is. Finding “disease genes” by only studying people who are already sick “risks inflating the numbers,” making a gene seem far more dangerous than it is for everyone else.

Working backwards means starting from the answer and reasoning back toward the cause — here, starting with people who already have a disease and then hunting for the gene they share. It sounds sensible, but it quietly stacks the deck: of course almost everyone in a group of sick people carries the “disease gene,” which makes the gene look scarier than it is in the general population.

A coined phrase for people labeled at risk of a disease they may never actually get — patients only in the sense that they're waiting to find out. Testing hundreds of low-penetrance genes could create crowds of these “patients-in-waiting,” carrying a scary label and the stress that comes with it for nothing.

A sticking-point is the one issue that snags an agreement — the obstacle everything gets stuck on. For many researchers and parents, storing a child's genome forever is the sticking-point: they might accept the disease-screening, but the idea of keeping that DNA indefinitely is where they dig in.

Indefinitely means for an unlimited time, with no set end — basically, forever, or at least with no promised stopping point. Storing a baby's genome “indefinitely” is one of the article's biggest worries, because that data could sit in a database long after anyone remembers agreeing to it.

A premium here is the price you pay for insurance — the regular fee, not “premium” meaning fancy. The fear is that some insurers could use your genetic-test results “when setting premiums,” charging you more because your DNA hints you might get sick someday.

Paternity is fatherhood — specifically the question of who a child's biological father actually is. Because DNA can settle that question, the article warns it could be used for blackmail, dredging up “questions of paternity” a family never wanted exposed.

“To boot” is an old-fashioned way to say “on top of that” or “as well” — nothing to do with footwear or computers. The trials are trying to do disease-screening and long-term research at once, “and with patients who are incapable of consenting to boot” — that is, and the patients can't even agree to it, in addition to everything else.

To flag something isn't to plant a flag — it's to mark or highlight it for attention, the way a teacher flags a mistake. DNA analysis can flag mutations that aren't causing trouble yet, and later flag people who might benefit from a new treatment — marking them out so someone takes a closer look.

To screen for a disease means to test lots of healthy people to catch a problem early — not a movie screen or a window screen. Many countries already screen newborns with a blood test; the debate here is whether to screen their whole DNA, which catches far more but also raises far more false alarms.

A trial here isn't a courtroom event — it's a carefully run test of whether something new (a treatment, or in this case a screening programme) actually works and is safe. Trials in America, Australia, and Europe are testing DNA screening on real newborns precisely to answer the hard questions the article raises.

A geneticist is a scientist who studies genes and how traits and diseases are passed down. The article leans on several of them — like the researcher who found that a supposedly 90%-dangerous eye-cancer gene rarely leads to cancer — because they're the ones who can tell how much a scary genetic result really means.

An inconclusive result doesn't settle anything — it's a “maybe,” neither a clear yes nor a clear no. The cystic-fibrosis label “screen positive inconclusive diagnosis” names exactly that limbo, and it's stressful enough that doctors gave it its own name.

To consent is to give informed permission — to say yes knowing what you're agreeing to. A newborn is “incapable of consenting,” which is the ethical knot at the heart of the story: parents are deciding, on a baby's behalf, to share the most personal information that baby has.

To equate two things is to treat them as equal or the same. The geneticist's point is that people have long “equated genetic information with certainty” — treating a gene result as a guaranteed fate — which she says is outdated now that we know how loosely many genes actually predict disease.

A rare cancer of the eye, mostly affecting young children. It opens the article as a success story — baby Freddie's was caught early thanks to genetic screening — but also as a caution, since the gene behind it turned out to cause the cancer far less often than doctors once believed.

A serious inherited disease that clogs the lungs and digestive system with thick mucus. It's the article's example of “diagnostic purgatory”: a screen can come back “positive but inconclusive,” leaving parents unsure for years whether their child truly has it.

A well-known company that mails you a spit kit and reads your DNA for ancestry and health clues. The article uses it as a warning: in 2023 hackers stole the genetic and personal information of 6.9 million of its customers — a reminder of what can go wrong when genomes are stored in one place.

An English programme that plans to sequence the complete DNA of 100,000 babies — the flagship example in this story. Its two goals sit at the heart of the debate: screen each baby for genetic disease now, and bank all that genomic data to power medical research later.
